Kwame worked as a nurse at a busy clinic in Accra, and all week his mind kept drifting to his mother's hospital tests back in Kumasi and his brother's school fees. By Wednesday he had almost handed a patient the wrong form. So he tried something. At the start of each shift, he wrote the worries on a card, "Ma's results. Kofi's fees," and put it in his locker. "Not now," he told himself. "At seven."
At seven each evening he sat on the porch with the card and a cup of tea for half an hour. He let himself worry, made one call if needed, and wrote down one next step. Some nights he cried a little. His wife, Rania, sat with him on Thursday. By the weekend he was sleeping better, and at work his mind stayed on the patient in front of him.

At the government school where he taught physics, Manoj had a rule this term. From the first bell to the last, his worries about his father's surgery stayed in a box. When a thought crept in during class, he jotted "Papa - later" on a scrap and pocketed it.
Then, at 3:40, after the final bell, he sat alone in the empty staffroom for twenty minutes. He took out the scraps, let himself feel scared, called the hospital or his sister, and wrote one thing he could do that evening.
His colleague Siddharth found him there one day, eyes red. "You okay?"
"This is my worry slot," Manoj said, and laughed shakily. "If I don't give it a time, it takes all my time."
Siddharth sat down. "Can I borrow the idea? My landlord situation is eating my brain."

qa.a: "Papa - later".

Dear Reena,
I know I've seemed far away lately. I want to explain, and to ask for something.
Since the restructuring at work was announced, I've been worrying about my job all day, every day, at the office and at home. I tried shoving it out of my head completely, but it just leaked out at 3 a.m.

Love,
Joseph
